messages.author: ff2a321e956a7e2a
messages.subject: SPDE priors
parts:
Dear group

I'm trying to find the inla.spde2.matern() default prior specifications. INLA help shows that prior.variance.nominal=1 by default, and there is no value for prior.range.nominal. In addition, theta.prior.prec=0.1, so I conclude that default priors are (in terms of precision)

log(tau)~N(1,01)
log(kappa)~N(?,0.1)

I have two main doubts

1) As theta_1 and theta_2 have a jointly normal distribution, does it means that (kappa default mean value) = (tau default mean value) = 1? Being a joint distribution, what if we wanted to assign a different prior means to kappa and tau?

2) In this thread

 https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/r-inla-discussion-group/spde$20$20default$20prior/r-inla-discussion-group/gIGkLLqCtpU/oppbQb5lb-4J

is stated that the priors are chosen heuristically to match the spatial scale of the mesh and that prior for the spde model can be seen in  spde$f$hyper.default. Does it mean that default priors are different for each mesh?

By typing that for my model, I get the output below.

spde$f$hyper.default
$theta1
$theta1$prior
[1] "mvnorm"

$theta1$param
[1]  7.479619 -8.745131  0.100000  0.000000  0.000000  0.100000

$theta1$initial
[1] 7.479619


$theta2
$theta2$initial
[1] -8.745131

How should I interpret this? Are the last four values related with precision matrix and two first related with approximation to kappa and tau mean? Then, what about initial 1 value? In relation with my first doubt, there are two different initial values for theta1 and theta2, how does this affect to mean of jointly normal distribution?

I apologize if they are too basic questions but my main training is as biologist and I'm a bit overwhelmed with math level used in INLA

Best regards

Marcial

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE priors
parts:
Hi,

Brief answer on point 2: yes, the default prior median for kappa depends on the mesh:
It computes the approximate diameter of the mesh, multiplies by 0.2 to get a value for the prior median range, and then transforms it to log-kappa scale by the formula
  log(sqrt(8*nu)/range)
where nu is alpha-dim/2.

I'm trying to find the inla.spde2.matern() default prior specifications. INLA help shows that prior.variance.nominal=1 by default, and there is no value for prior.range.nominal. In addition, theta.prior.prec=0.1, so I conclude that default priors are (in terms of precision)

log(tau)~N(1,01)
log(kappa)~N(?,0.1)
N(.., 10), yes.  (Variance =1 / precision)

I have two main doubts

1) As theta_1 and theta_2 have a jointly normal distribution, does it means that (kappa default mean value) = (tau default mean value) = 1? Being a joint distribution, what if we wanted to assign a different prior means to kappa and tau?

Log tau and log kappa are both linear combinations (specified with B.tau and B.kappa) of a common set of Multivariate gaussian theta parameters (by default; the distribution can actually be overridden by the user using the generic prior specification methods, but it's a bit messy).  This means that one can either have two subsets of theta each controlling either tau or kappa, or one can have some theta controlling aspects of both tau and kappa.  This allows, for example, direct control over variance and range.  See the "read this first" tutorial text on spde models on the R-inla.org website for examples.

2) In this thread

 https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/r-inla-discussion-group/spde$20$20default$20prior/r-inla-discussion-group/gIGkLLqCtpU/oppbQb5lb-4J

is stated that the priors are chosen heuristically to match the spatial scale of the mesh and that prior for the spde model can be seen in  spde$f$hyper.default. Does it mean that default priors are different for each mesh?
Yes, see above.

By typing that for my model, I get the output below.

spde$f$hyper.default
$theta1
$theta1$prior
[1] "mvnorm"

$theta1$param
[1]  7.479619 -8.745131  0.100000  0.000000  0.000000  0.100000

$theta1$initial
[1] 7.479619


$theta2
$theta2$initial
[1] -8.745131

How should I interpret this? Are the last four values related with precision matrix and two first related with approximation to kappa and tau mean? Then, what about initial 1 value? In relation with my first doubt, there are two different initial values for theta1 and theta2, how does this affect to mean of jointly normal distribution?

I apologize if they are too basic questions but my main training is as biologist and I'm a bit overwhelmed with math level used in INLA

Best regards

Marcial

parts:
Hi again

    After reading Finn's answer and suggested tutorial my conclusions are:

    Let f(s) the spatial effect included in my model; then

    f(s)~N(0,Q^-1)

    where Q is an i x j precision matrix which depends on tau and kappa. Kappa depends in turn on the size of the specific mesh used in my model, so Q^-1 will be different for any mesh. Both tau and kappa are linear combinations of a set of theta; the set of theta follows a multivariate normal distribution and that would be the reason why f(s) is multivariate normal too. We define prior distribution on theta set.

Is this correct? I fso, which prior would be defined by default in INLA? log Gamma(0, 5e-5) for any theta, as is for other parameters? N(0,0.1)?


Greetings

Marcial

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE priors
parts:
On 18/01/15 10:29, Marcial Marín wrote:
> Let f(s) the spatial effect included in my model; then
>
> f(s)~N(0,Q^-1)
>
> where Q is an i x j precision matrix which depends on tau and
> kappa. Kappa depends in turn on the size of the specific mesh used in my
> model, so Q^-1 will be different for any mesh.

The default _prior_ for kappa depends on the mesh, yes. Q is based on
basis functions on the mesh, so inherently depends on the mesh.

> Both tau and kappa are
> linear combinations of a set of theta;
log(tau) and log(kappa), yes. Not tau and kappa themselves.

> the set of theta follows a
> multivariate normal distribution
Yes.

> and that would be the reason why f(s)
> is multivariate normal too.

No, f(s) _conditionally_ on tau and kappa (i.e. on theta) is
multivariate Gaussian regardless of what prior is put on theta.
> We define prior distribution on theta set.

Yes.

> Is this correct?

Partly yes, partly no, as detailed above.

> I fso, which prior would be defined by default in INLA?
> log Gamma(0, 5e-5) for any theta, as is for other parameters? N(0,0.1)?

As per previous email, inla.spe2.matern by default attempts to set a
sensible prior median for the spatial correlation range, by choosing
the prior mean of the theta vector. The user needs to help by
specifying a sensible prior median for the variance, via
prior.variance.nominal. The _precision_ for theta is by default 0.1,
which means that the standard deviation of each theta component is
approximately 3. Note that this is in the _log_ scale for tau and
kappa, so it's related to the _relative_ deviation from the prior median.

Finn
